notes:
I have gathered substantial material from Enduring Word, Precept Austin, GTY (MacArthur), Desiring God (Piper), Ellicott, Gill, Wesley, Spurgeon, NET notes, and Calvin. Here are the notes, verse by verse.

---

## John 15 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: "I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard."

**Traditional Reading:**

- This is the seventh and last of Jesus' "I AM" statements in John, a claim to deity echoing Exodus 3:14. The word "true" (*alēthinos*) means genuine, real, as opposed to counterfeit — Jesus is the reality of which Israel's vine was only a shadow. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/43-79/i-am-the-true-vine)
- In the OT, Israel is repeatedly pictured as God's vine (Ps 80:8–9; Isa 5:1–7; Jer 2:21; Hos 10:1), but Israel proved unfaithful and fruitless. Jesus now declares *Himself* to be the true vine — He displaces Israel as the source of divine life and blessing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- The imagery may have been prompted by the "fruit of the vine" just consumed at the Last Supper, or by the golden vine carved on the temple gates (Josephus). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/15.htm)
- The Father as vinedresser (*geōrgos*, "farmer, one who tills the soil") is the owner-cultivator with full control over the vine and branches. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-15-commentary)

**Tradition Distinctives:**

- **Reformed (Calvin):** The Father plants the elect by special grace; the commencement of life is in Christ alone. Men toil in vain seeking strength anywhere else. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-15-commentary)
- **Baptist (MacArthur):** Jesus is the *true* vine in contrast to Israel, the degenerate, dead vine. Life flows only through Christ; connection to Israel or religious heritage saves no one. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/43-79/i-am-the-true-vine)
- **Wesleyan (Wesley):** "I am the true vine — So the true bread, John 6:32; that is, the most excellent." Jesus is the preeminent vine, the finest. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

**Other Views:**

- **NET Bible notes (modern scholarship):** The vine was a symbol of Israel on Maccabean coins. The OT passages using vine imagery for Israel emphasize faithlessness and judgment. Jesus' self-description as the true vine "differs significantly from OT concepts; it appears to be original with Jesus." The imagery underscores that fruitfulness results not from human achievement but from one's position in Christ. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-15-commentary)

---

### v. 2: "He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful."

**Traditional Reading:**

- "Every branch in Me" — the unfruitful branches are those *in Christ* by outward profession but not by living union. The Father "takes away" (Greek *airō*) such branches. Some (Boice, Tenney) argue *airō* may be better translated "lifts up" (as vinedressers lift trailing vines off the ground for better sun exposure), though most traditional commentators read it as removal/judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- The fruitful branches are "pruned" (Greek *kathairō*, also meaning "cleansed"). Pruning involves cutting away shoots that waste energy and removing everything hindering growth. In the spiritual life, this means God uses suffering, discipline, and the Word to remove impediments to fruitfulness. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/15.htm)
- Ellicott: "We are not to interpret these words...of the unbelieving world, or of the Jews; but of Christians in name, who claim to be branches of the true vine." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/15.htm)

**Tradition Distinctives:**

- **Arminian/Wesleyan:** Wesley teaches that the unfruitful branches were once truly united to Christ by living faith but may be cut off — the passage is a warning against falling away. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-15-commentary)
- **Reformed/Calvinist (majority):** The unfruitful branches represent professing believers who were never genuinely saved — like Judas. They were attached outwardly but had no spiritual life. This view preserves eternal security. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/43-79/i-am-the-true-vine)
- **Reformed/Calvinist (minority):** Some Reformed interpreters hold the unfruitful branches are *true* believers who lose not salvation but rewards and usefulness (like Lot). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-15-commentary)
- **Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Fruitlessness proves the branch was never truly in saving union. John 15 does not contradict eternal security or perseverance; it warns that true saving union is more than church membership or ministry — it is bearing the fruit of love. (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/does-john-15-defy-calvinism)

---

### v. 3: "You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you."

**Traditional Reading:**

- "Clean" translates the same Greek root (*kathairō*) as "prune" in v. 2. Jesus tells the eleven they have already undergone an initial cleansing through His word — connecting back to John 13:10 ("you are clean, though not all of you"). The Word of God is the pruning instrument. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Wesley: "All of you, to whom I now speak, are purged from the guilt and power of sin; by the word — Which, applied by the Spirit, is the grand instrument of purifying the soul." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)
- Gill: The word spoken by Christ has a cleansing, sanctifying power in believers, separating them from the world. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/15.htm)

**Tradition Distinctives:**

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** The word is a cleansing agent — it condemns sin, inspires holiness, promotes growth, and reveals power for victory. Jesus continues to wash His people through the word (Eph 5:26). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** "Ye are clean (or pruned) through the word which I have spoken unto you. It is the word that prunes the Christian, it is the truth that purges him." (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-sharp-knife-for-the-vine-branches)

---

### v. 4: "Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me."

**Traditional Reading:**

- "Abide" (*menō*) is the key verb of the chapter — used 12 times. It denotes a continuing, active, conscious relationship of dependence, not a one-time event. The abiding is mutual: the disciple in Christ and Christ in the disciple. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Ellicott: "The branch regarded of itself, apart from the vine, has no original source of life. The sap flows from the vine to branch and tendril and leaf and fruit." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/15.htm)
- Boice (quoted at Enduring Word): "When our Lord says: Abide in me he is talking about the will, about the choices, the decisions we make. We must decide to do things which expose ourselves to him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

**Tradition Distinctives:**

- **Wesleyan:** Abiding is by "living faith, producing all holiness; by which alone ye can be in me." Faith is not a static possession but must be actively maintained. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 5: "I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Jesus states the relationship explicitly: He is the vine, they are the branches. The result of mutual abiding is "much fruit." "Apart from Me" (Greek *chōris emou*, "separate from Me") — the disciple can do nothing of eternal value without Christ. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Ellicott: The words "have often been unduly pressed, to exclude all moral power apart from Christ, whereas the whole context limits them to the fruit-bearing of the Christian life." Moral power outside Christianity is recognized in the NT (Rom 2:14–15). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/15.htm)
- Spurgeon: "The 'I am' comes out in the personal word 'me,' and the claim of all power unveils the Omnipotent. These words mean Godhead or nothing." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Trench: "It is only by union with Him that any branch can bear fruit: once that union is broken, the sap no longer flows." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

### v. 6: "If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away and withers. Such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burned."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The progression is sobering: cast out → withered → gathered → thrown → burned. This is a warning of judgment. The imagery of burning carries associations of final punishment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Gill: The one who does not abide is "cast forth as a branch" — ejected from the visible church, withers in his profession, and finally perishes. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/15.htm)
- Ellicott emphasizes that the verbs shift from past to present tense, viewing the final judgment as already certain: "they burn." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/15.htm)

**Tradition Distinctives (the key divide):**

- **Arminian/Wesleyan:** Wesley says, "If any one abide not in me — By living faith; not by Church communion only. He may thus abide in Christ, and be withered all the time, and cast into the fire at last. He is cast out — Of the vineyard, the invisible Church. Therefore he was in it once." This supports the view that true believers can fall away. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)
- **Reformed/Baptist (MacArthur):** The unfruitful, burned branches represent false disciples like Judas — people who appeared attached but never had spiritual life. True believers persevere and cannot be lost (John 10:28–29). (https://www.gty.org/sermons/43-79/i-am-the-true-vine)
- **Piper (Reformed Baptist):** "There is an abiding that is real, and there is an artificial grafting that is not real." The warning is against false assurance, not genuine salvation being lost. (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/does-john-15-defy-calvinism)

---

### v. 7: "If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Abiding in Christ is linked to His *words* abiding in the disciple. This is not a blank cheque for selfish desires but a promise that the one whose will is shaped by Christ's words will pray in harmony with God's will. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Ellicott: Jesus passes from the figure; "The abiding of His words in them is the means by which, and the proof that they do abide in Him." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/15.htm)
- Spurgeon: "Prayer comes spontaneously from those who abide in Jesus… Prayer is the natural outgushing of a soul in communion with Jesus." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

**Tradition Distinctives:**

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic:** The connection between abiding and answered prayer is a central promise for Spirit-filled living. Faithful abiding disciples should expect answered prayer; failure to see answers signals something amiss in the relationship. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

### v. 8: "This is to My Father's glory, that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Fruit-bearing glorifies the Father — the vinedresser is honoured by a fruitful vine. The disciple who bears "much fruit" demonstrates (proves) genuine discipleship. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Carson (quoted at Enduring Word): "Genuine conversion is not measured by the hasty decision but by long-range fruitfulness." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Ellicott suggests an alternative reading: "In this doing whatever ye ask, my Father is glorified, in order that ye may bear much fruit, and that ye may become my disciples." The answered prayer itself glorifies God and leads to fruit and confirmed discipleship. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 9: "As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The comparison is staggering: the love Jesus has for His disciples is patterned on the Father's love for the Son — eternal, measureless, unchanging, intimate. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Morgan (quoted at Enduring Word): "This surely is Christ's superlative word concerning His love for His own. It leaves nothing more to be said." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- The command to "remain in My love" signals that the disciple must actively maintain their place in the conscious enjoyment of Christ's love. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 10: "If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love, just as I have kept My Father's commandments and remain in His love."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Abiding in Christ's love is not a mystical feeling but is demonstrated through obedience to His commandments. Jesus models this: He kept the Father's commandments and thus abode in the Father's love. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Morris (quoted at Enduring Word): "This is not some mystical experience. It is simple obedience. It is when a man keeps Christ's commandments that he abides in Christ's love." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

**Tradition Distinctives:**

- **Wesleyan:** Wesley calls v. 14 "a thunderbolt for Antinomianism! Who then dares assert that God's love does not at all depend on man's works?" Obedience is the condition for remaining in Christ's love. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 11: "I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The "joy of Jesus" is His own holy exultation in the consciousness of the Father's love (Alford). It is not mere happiness but the deep exhilaration of being right with God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Clarke: The joy is "filled up — a metaphor taken from a vessel, into which water is poured till it is full to the brim." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Spurgeon: "God made human beings, as he made his other creatures, to be happy… now that Jesus Christ has come to restore the ruins of the Fall, he has to bring back to us the old joy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

### v. 12: "This is My commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you."

**Traditional Reading:**

- This repeats the new commandment from John 13:34. "As I have loved you" sets the standard: sacrificial, servant-hearted, initiating love. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

### v. 13: "Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The supreme demonstration of love is self-sacrifice unto death. Jesus speaks here of love for *friends* specifically (Wesley notes this limitation). The cross is the ultimate expression. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 14: "You are My friends if you do what I command you."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Friendship with Jesus is conditional upon obedience — not as earning favour, but as evidence of genuine relationship. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Wesley: "Ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you — On this condition, not otherwise. A thunderbolt for Antinomianism!" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 15: "No longer do I call you servants, for a servant does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The elevation from servant to friend is grounded in revelation: Jesus has shared with the disciples everything the Father gave Him. A servant merely obeys orders without understanding; a friend is brought into the master's confidence. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- This does not mean the disciples cease to serve; it means their service is now transformed by intimate knowledge of God's purposes. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 16: "You did not choose Me, but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain—so that whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Election is emphasized: the initiative is entirely Christ's. The disciples' privileges (friendship, answered prayer, fruit-bearing) are rooted in His choice, not their merit. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- The purpose of election is fruit-bearing — "fruit that will remain" (lasting, eternal results). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Wesley applies "ye" specifically to the apostles: "Ye — My apostles, have not chosen me, but I have chosen you — As clearly appears from the sacred history: and appointed you, that ye may go and bear fruit — I have chosen and appointed you for this end, that ye may go and convert sinners." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

**Tradition Distinctives:**

- **Reformed:** The verse strongly supports unconditional election — "You did not choose Me, but I chose you." Salvation is entirely God's initiative. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-15-commentary)
- **Wesleyan:** Wesley connects fruit-bearing to conversion of sinners and prayer being heard as a consequence of going and bearing fruit — the scope is missional. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 17: "This is My command to you: Love one another."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Jesus repeats the command to love for emphasis. When He departs, the disciples must not disband or turn against each other. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

### v. 18: "If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first."

**Traditional Reading:**

- "The world" (*kosmos*) here denotes humanity organised in opposition to God. The disciples should not be surprised by hatred; it came to Jesus first. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

### v. 19: "If you were of the world, it would love you as its own. Instead, the world hates you, because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The world loves its own. Hatred from the world is actually evidence that the disciples belong to Christ, not the world. Being "chosen out of the world" explains both their status and the world's hostility. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Wesley: "Because your maxims, tempers, actions, are quite opposite to theirs. For the very same reason must the world in all ages hate those who are not of the world." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 20: "Remember the word that I spoke to you: 'No servant is greater than his master.' If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well; if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Jesus quotes His earlier saying (John 13:16). Persecution of the disciples is inevitable because it mirrors what was done to the Master. Yet there is also hope: some kept Jesus' word, and some will keep the disciples' word too. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

### v. 21: "But they will treat you like this because of My name, since they do not know the One who sent Me."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The root cause of persecution is ignorance of God. Hatred of Jesus' followers stems from not knowing the Father who sent Him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Wesley: "In all ages and nations they who know not God will, for this cause, hate and persecute those that do." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 22: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not be guilty of sin. Now, however, they have no excuse for their sin."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Jesus' coming and speaking increased the accountability of those who heard and rejected Him. The sin here is specifically the sin of unbelief and rejection of Christ's words. Before His clear revelation, they had ignorance as mitigation; now they have "no excuse" (literally, "no cloak" to cover their sin). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Wesley: "They had not had sin — Not in this respect." — i.e., not the specific sin of rejecting Christ. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

---

### v. 23: "Whoever hates Me hates My Father as well."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The unity of Father and Son is such that rejection of Jesus is simultaneously rejection of God the Father. One cannot claim to love God while hating Jesus. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

### v. 24: "If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin; but now they have seen and hated both Me and My Father."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Jesus' miraculous works provided unmistakable evidence of His divine origin. Having seen these works and still hated Him, their guilt is compounded. The works left them without excuse, just as the words did (v. 22). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

### v. 25: "But this is to fulfill what is written in their Law: 'They hated Me without reason.'"

**Traditional Reading:**

- Jesus cites Psalm 69:4 (or possibly Psalm 35:19). "Their Law" refers to the Jewish Scriptures as a whole. The hatred against Jesus — and by extension His disciples — is irrational and undeserved, fulfilling OT prophecy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

### v. 26: "When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father — the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father — He will testify about Me."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The "Advocate" (Greek *paraklētos*, also "Helper, Comforter") is the Holy Spirit. He is called "the Spirit of truth" and is sent by Jesus from the Father. The phrase "who proceeds from the Father" speaks to the Spirit's eternal origin and divine nature. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)
- Wesley: "The Spirit's coming, and being sent by our Lord from the Father, to testify of him, are personal characters, and plainly distinguish him from the Father and the Son; and his title as the Spirit of truth, together with his proceeding from the Father, can agree to none but a Divine person. And that he proceeds from the Son, as well as from the Father, may be fairly argued from his being called the Spirit of Christ, 1Pet 1:11." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/15.htm)

**Tradition Distinctives:**

- **Eastern Orthodox vs. Roman Catholic (the *Filioque*):** The clause "who proceeds from the Father" is central to the historic debate over the *Filioque* ("and the Son"). The Eastern Orthodox Church holds that the Spirit proceeds from the Father *alone*, citing this verse. The Roman Catholic Church (and most Protestants) teaches that the Spirit proceeds from the Father *and the Son*, appealing to v. 26's statement that Jesus "will send" the Spirit. *[Note: I was unable to fetch pages from oca.org, newadvent.org, or catholic.com due to search/fetch limits. The existence of this dispute is well-known, but I cannot cite a specific page from those sites describing their reading of this verse.]*

---

### v. 27: "And you also must testify, because you have been with Me from the beginning."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The Spirit's testimony is primary; the disciples' witness is secondary but essential. They are qualified as eyewitnesses — "you have been with Me from the beginning" of His public ministry. The Spirit testifies inwardly and through the apostles' preaching. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-15/)

---

## Summary of Major Tradition Differences on John 15

| Issue | Reformed/Baptist (MacArthur, Piper) | Arminian/Wesleyan (Wesley) |
|---|---|---|
| **Unfruitful branches (vv. 2, 6)** | False professors, never truly saved (like Judas) | True believers who can fall away and be lost |
| **Security of the believer** | The elect persevere; John 10:28–29 guarantees eternal security | Abiding must be maintained by living faith; falling away is possible |
| **Election (v. 16)** | Unconditional — God's sovereign choice alone | Christ chose the apostles particularly; emphasis on human response |
| **Obedience and love (vv. 10, 14)** | Obedience is evidence of genuine union | Obedience is the *condition* for remaining in Christ's love |

*(Source for comparison framework: https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-15-commentary)*
